entries.title: France’s $4T Debt Crisis, SpaceX’s $40B AI Debt, and Lucid’s EV Backlog — Wednesday, October 7, 2026
entries.description: Wednesday, October 7, 2026
entries.body:
Wednesday, October 7, 2026

Today's Numbers

• $4 Trillion: Total national debt carried by France—amounting to roughly 120 percent of its annual economic output—triggering nationwide school blockades and investor anxiety over a $100 billion annual debt-servicing tab. (The New York Times)

• $40 Billion: The massive new debt load SpaceX is reportedly taking on to purchase cutting-edge Nvidia AI processors, leaving the space rocket and satellite giant carrying five times more leverage than Alphabet relative to profits. (Semafor)

• 3,806 Vehicles: Electric cars delivered by Lucid Motors in the third quarter, falling well short of Wall Street targets of 4,700 and forcing the automaker to cut factory shifts to shrink inventory. (Robinhood Snacks)

• 250,000 Demonstrators: The minimum number of students, teachers, and union workers who marched across 40 French cities protesting school understaffing, crumbling classrooms, and government austerity budgets. (The New York Times)

• $35,820 (£27,100): The record-setting auction price paid for a premier working sheepdog, highlighting how sheep farmers regularly pay more for top-pedigree border collies than new automobiles. (Semafor)

• 20,000 Copies: Sales tally for August Lamm's expanded analog zine You Don't Need a Smartphone as the former influencer leads sold-out "downgrading" events across New York. (After School)

• 1,500 Students: The cohort of high schoolers surveyed in a new cognitive study finding that heavy short-form video consumption erodes teenagers' ability to connect present effort with future rewards. (After School via The Wall Street Journal)

• 105 Million: Monthly active visitors on Amazon's Twitch streaming platform, where the company is launching live QVC-style shopping carousels to capture Gen Z buyers. (After School)

Quotes of the Day

• "Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella aren't slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and won't stop spending until their shareholders make them." — Liz Hoffman, business editor, analyzing the relentless AI infrastructure capital expenditure boom across Silicon Valley, via Semafor

• "Leaders should be prepared to call out Russia and be candid with their citizens about these dangers, the nature of the struggle and how Russian threats are best addressed." — Lawrence Freedman, emeritus professor of war studies at King's College London, on escalating European security tensions, via The New York Times

• "We're not tone-deaf to our customers." — General Motors executive, confirming that the automaker is introducing more hybrid vehicle options to its U.S. consumer lineup as drivers shy away from pure battery EVs, via Robinhood Snacks

• "If agents are going to become computer users, why do their computers need to look anything like ours?" — Joanna Stern, technology columnist, examining why autonomous artificial intelligence agents run on headless cloud Linux virtual machines rather than human desktop screens, via The New Things

• "I haven't really located the source of the malaise." — Anonymous 26-year-old attendee, carrying two smartphones at a sold-out New York digital downgrading workshop while comparing mobile phone use to chemical dependency, via After School

Business, Capital & Tech Infrastructure

SpaceX Embarks on $40 Billion Debt Binge to Fund Nvidia AI Chip Purchases

Elon Musk's SpaceX is reportedly raising $40 billion in corporate debt to purchase specialized Nvidia artificial intelligence processors. While revenue from Starlink satellites helps support SpaceX's expensive rocket operations, the company carries five times more debt than Alphabet and three times more than Meta relative to profits. Because SpaceX went public in June with a BBB credit rating, issuing new equity or securing cheap bonds has become more challenging, pushing the company toward specialized private credit lenders like Apollo to finance its mounting AI computing commitments. Read the complete corporate finance analysis on Semafor.Elon Musk's aerospace giant takes on heavy corporate debt to compete in the frontier AI infrastructure race.

Private Credit Giants Face Investor Lawsuits Over Inflated Asset Valuations

Major private credit managers, including Blue Owl, FS KKR, and Ares, are facing lawsuits from pension funds and institutional investors accusing the firms of inflating fund asset valuations. The complaints allege that the asset managers used payment-in-kind arrangements—which let distressed corporate borrowers delay cash interest payments—to paper over bad debts and artificially inflate performance fees. The legal challenges coincide with increased regulatory scrutiny, as the Securities and Exchange Commission and Federal Reserve audit commercial bank exposure to private credit markets. Read the investigative report on Semafor.Pension funds sue leading non-bank lenders over deferred interest payments and steep management fees.

Global Affairs & Geopolitics

France Plunges into Financial and Social Crisis as Debt Reaches $4 Trillion

Cascading student strikes, port blockades, and soaring bond yields rattle Paris ahead of spring elections.

France is confronting an escalating wave of social unrest and financial instability as public demonstrations expand across more than 40 cities. High school and university students launched school blockades over crumbling infrastructure and understaffed classrooms, drawing support from striking labor unions and mariners protesting surging fuel costs. The unrest comes as France's national debt approaches 120 percent of gross domestic product, requiring nearly $100 billion next year just to service interest payments. Financial markets fear the spending cuts proposed by President Emmanuel Macron will deepen political gridlock ahead of next spring's presidential contest. Read the full Paris dispatch in The New York Times.

China's Alternative Interbank Payment Network Surges to Record Volume

China's cross-border interbank payment system, known as CIPS, logged record daily transaction volume in August as international companies increasingly settle trade without touching the U.S. dollar. While new data from the Atlantic Council confirms that the greenback still underpins the vast majority of global foreign-exchange reserves and commercial transactions, the number of direct participants in CIPS has more than doubled since Western allies froze Russian central bank assets. Developing economies are increasingly tapping Beijing's central-bank currency swap lines to bypass American financial jurisdiction. Review the global currency analysis in Semafor.Beijing's cross-border financial rail expands as sanctioned global firms seek workarounds to U.S. dollar dominance.

Culture & Consumer Trends

The Luddite Influencer of New York: Ditching the Smartphone for a 2002 Nokia

Former social media influencer August Lamm, who once commanded 200,000 digital followers, traded her iPhone for a vintage 2002 Nokia phone, pawned her laptop, and published You Don't Need a Smartphone. Her sold-out "downgrading" workshops in Manhattan draw crowds of young professionals desperate to break smartphone addiction and reclaim mental focus from algorithmic feeds. Read the cultural report in After School via The New York Times.Former digital creator August Lamm leads sold-out workshops teaching young adults to embrace analog devices.

Amazon Turns Twitch into a QVC Live-Shopping Hub for Gen Z

Ahead of Prime Day, Amazon introduced live shopping streams to Twitch, testing interactive product carousels for blenders and apparel. With over 70 percent of Twitch's 105 million monthly visitors between ages 18 and 34, Amazon is pushing to catch up with social shopping competitors like TikTok Shop and Whatnot as younger generations embrace live e-commerce. Read the retail dispatch in After School.Interactive retail carousels arrive on gaming livestreams ahead of fall discount holidays.

Automotive & Mobility

Lucid Motors Cuts Production Shifts as Unsold Electric Cars Pile Up

American electric vehicle manufacturer Lucid Motors delivered only 3,806 luxury sedans in the third quarter, missing Wall Street expectations of 4,700 vehicles. Manufacturing output dropped 38 percent from the prior quarter to 2,954 vehicles as the company actively dialed back assembly lines. New chief executive Silvio Napoli, who took the helm in June, eliminated a second production shift at the company's Arizona plant to clear excess inventory and target $1.4 billion in annual cash-flow improvements. While competitors Tesla and Rivian beat delivery estimates, legacy automakers like General Motors and Toyota are pivoting toward hybrids to satisfy cautious consumers. Read the automotive breakdown on Robinhood Snacks.The luxury EV maker misses quarterly delivery estimates, forcing factory cutbacks to stem cash burn.

Software, AI & Security

Western AI Startups Challenge Chinese Open-Source Dominance with 'Beam' and 'Le Chonk'

David Robinson, the computer scientist responsible for drafting OpenAI's internal risk assessment and safety protocols, resigned from the artificial intelligence laboratory over governance and safety concerns. Speaking on The Ezra Klein Show, Robinson explained that commercial competition and investor expectations are overriding deliberate safety testing, echoing broader whistleblower warnings across the industry. The high-profile departure comes as federal lawmakers debate new statutory risk-reporting rules for frontier AI developers. Listen to the interview on The New York Times.Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French AI lab Mistral release open-weights models as enterprise pilots expire.

Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French artificial intelligence lab Mistral released new open-weights language models designed to counter Chinese open-source AI market share. With enterprise IT budgets facing intense end-of-year reviews as introductory $1 pilot deals expire, corporate software buyers in heavily regulated industries and government agencies are seeking Western open-source models that bypass both Chinese models and costly proprietary cloud APIs. Read the venture analysis on Semafor.

AI Agents Take Over Linux Virtual Machines in the Cloud

Autonomous assistants leave behind physical desktop monitors to live inside headless server racks.

Tech columnist Joanna Stern investigated the backend infrastructure powering autonomous artificial intelligence assistants like OpenAI's Dot and Meta's Muse. Rather than operating on physical computers or human desktop interfaces, these agents run around the clock inside isolated cloud Linux virtual machines. Because AI software does not rely on visual monitors or mouse clicks, engineers are questioning whether computer operating systems built for autonomous agents should abandon human-centered desktop metaphors entirely. Read the technical analysis in The New Things.

OpenAI Safety Architect David Robinson Resigns Over Guardrail Concerns

The author of the startup's safety protocols departs, warning about internal pressure to ship frontier models prematurely.

Google Secures 20-Year Nuclear Power Agreement with Constellation Energy

Google signed a landmark 20-year clean energy agreement with Constellation Energy to procure baseline nuclear power for its artificial intelligence data centers. The long-term pact mirrors recent agreements struck by Microsoft and NextEra Energy as tech giants confront strained regional electrical grids. With frontier computing clusters requiring gigawatts of continuous power, hyperscalers are increasingly purchasing entire reactor outputs to keep server campuses online without relying on fossil fuel peaker plants. Read the energy brief on Robinhood Snacks.Hyperscale tech firms turn to dedicated nuclear reactors to provide round-the-clock electricity for AI clusters.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• DeepSeek Targets $12 Billion Valuation in Tencent-Backed Round: Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek opened talks to raise new growth capital with financial backing from tech giant Tencent to expand its open-weights model development. Read the venture report on Robinhood Snacks.

• Skydance Media Credit Rating Downgraded by Fitch: Credit agency Fitch downgraded the corporate debt of David Ellison's Skydance Media following its blockbuster merger with Paramount and Warner Bros., citing heavy debt loads and soft theatrical box office receipts. Read the credit notice on Robinhood Snacks.

• Lionel Messi Plays Final Match for Argentina: Global soccer superstar Lionel Messi played his final international contest for the Argentina national team, concluding a legendary twenty-year international career featuring two Copa América trophies and the 2022 World Cup. Read the sports tribute in The New York Times.

• U.S. Trade Deficit Hits 17-Month High: Federal commerce statistics revealed that the United States trade deficit expanded to its widest margin in 17 months as strong consumer demand for imported goods outweighed export gains. Check the economic indicator in The New York Times.

• GEICO Gecko Celebrates 27-Year Advertising Legacy: Robinhood Snacks highlighted the 1999 debut of GEICO's iconic animated mascot, which originally appeared pleading with television audiences to stop calling him for car insurance. Explore the brand profile on Robinhood Snacks.

• Headphones Blamed for Gen Z Disconnection: Essayist Sam Matthews Boehmer argues that constant earbud use is eroding youth social interaction and contemplation, leaving young adults unable to tolerate quiet reflection without background audio. • 1,500 Students: The cohort of high schoolers surveyed in a new cognitive study finding that heavy short-form video consumption erodes teenagers' ability to connect present effort with future rewards. (After School via The Wall Street Journal)

• 105 Million: Monthly active visitors on Amazon's Twitch streaming platform, where the company is launching live QVC-style shopping carousels to capture Gen Z buyers. (After School)

Quotes of the Day

• "Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella aren't slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and won't stop spending until their shareholders make them." — Liz Hoffman, business editor, analyzing the relentless AI infrastructure capital expenditure boom across Silicon Valley, via Semafor

• "Leaders should be prepared to call out Russia and be candid with their citizens about these dangers, the nature of the struggle and how Russian threats are best addressed." — Lawrence Freedman, emeritus professor of war studies at King's College London, on escalating European security tensions, via The New York Times

• "We're not tone-deaf to our customers." — General Motors executive, confirming that the automaker is introducing more hybrid vehicle options to its U.S. consumer lineup as drivers shy away from pure battery EVs, via Robinhood Snacks

• "If agents are going to become computer users, why do their computers need to look anything like ours?" — Joanna Stern, technology columnist, examining why autonomous artificial intelligence agents run on headless cloud Linux virtual machines rather than human desktop screens, via The New Things

• "I haven't really located the source of the malaise." — Anonymous 26-year-old attendee, carrying two smartphones at a sold-out New York digital downgrading workshop while comparing mobile phone use to chemical dependency, via After School

SpaceX Embarks on $40 Billion Debt Binge to Fund Nvidia AI Chip Purchases

While revenue from Starlink satellites helps support SpaceX's expensive rocket operations, the company carries five times more debt than Alphabet and three times more than Meta relative to profits. Because SpaceX went public in June with a BBB credit rating, issuing new equity or securing cheap bonds has become more challenging, pushing the company toward specialized private credit lenders like Apollo to finance its mounting AI computing commitments. Read the complete corporate finance analysis on Semafor.Elon Musk's aerospace giant takes on heavy corporate debt to compete in the frontier AI infrastructure race.

Private Credit Giants Face Investor Lawsuits Over Inflated Asset Valuations

Major private credit managers, including Blue Owl, FS KKR, and Ares, are facing lawsuits from pension funds and institutional investors accusing the firms of inflating fund asset valuations. The complaints allege that the asset managers used payment-in-kind arrangements—which let distressed corporate borrowers delay cash interest payments—to paper over bad debts and artificially inflate performance fees. The legal challenges coincide with increased regulatory scrutiny, as the Securities and Exchange Commission and Federal Reserve audit commercial bank exposure to private credit markets. Read the investigative report on Semafor.Pension funds sue leading non-bank lenders over deferred interest payments and steep management fees.

Global Affairs & Geopolitics

France Plunges into Financial and Social Crisis as Debt Reaches $4 Trillion

Cascading student strikes, port blockades, and soaring bond yields rattle Paris ahead of spring elections.

France is confronting an escalating wave of social unrest and financial instability as public demonstrations expand across more than 40 cities. High school and university students launched school blockades over crumbling infrastructure and understaffed classrooms, drawing support from striking labor unions and mariners protesting surging fuel costs. The unrest comes as France's national debt approaches 120 percent of gross domestic product, requiring nearly $100 billion next year just to service interest payments. Financial markets fear the spending cuts proposed by President Emmanuel Macron will deepen political gridlock ahead of next spring's presidential contest. Read the full Paris dispatch in The New York Times.

China's Alternative Interbank Payment Network Surges to Record Volume

China's cross-border interbank payment system, known as CIPS, logged record daily transaction volume in August as international companies increasingly settle trade without touching the U.S. dollar. While new data from the Atlantic Council confirms that the greenback still underpins the vast majority of global foreign-exchange reserves and commercial transactions, the number of direct participants in CIPS has more than doubled since Western allies froze Russian central bank assets. Developing economies are increasingly tapping Beijing's central-bank currency swap lines to bypass American financial jurisdiction. entries.description: Thursday, October 8, 2026 - Evening Edition
entries.body:
Thursday, October 8, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• **90-foot**: the height of the lava-rock arch that collapsed this week in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park after a tropical storm tore through. The Park Service says it was cut from a 550-year-old lava flow. Nature does not sit still.

• **31%**: the share of U.S. adults who now say a college education is "very important," per a new Gallup survey. A credential that used to be a given is now a genuine debate.

• **42 minutes**: how long it took Glastonbury to sell out this year. Ticket inflation is real and the frenzy is back.

• **$100M**: the value of art Jeff Koons is reportedly selling from his personal collection. When the market gets shaky, the trophy room gets sold.

• **30%**: the jump in print and digital subscriptions at Georgia's Monticello News, six weeks after 25-year-old Evan Newton bought the paper with his entire savings. Local news might be boring, but it is necessary (his words).

• **230mg**: the caffeine packed into a 10-gummy pack of Five-Hour Energy's new candy-style gummies. Halloween candy for your friend who crushes Celsius all day.

• **$3 billion**: Grindr is now a $3 billion company, and it is lobbying Washington. The hookup app has a K Street playbook.

Quotes of the Day

• "Let's do the fucking news!" (Bari Weiss, the real answer in Hunter Harris's "Who Said That: Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy" quiz)

• "If you want something done, give it to a busy mom." (Maria Dueñas Jacobs, founder of Super Smalls, in a founder interview)

• "exclusivity is not the objective" (Arnaud Frisch, founder of Paris nightclub Silencio, on what makes a nightclub an institution)

• "everyone everywhere is just trying to make One Big Bet and Get Rich Quick" (Emily Sundberg, summarizing Max Read's theory that everything is gambling now)

• "All of Berlin hates Anna and Tom, but all of Berlin also is Anna and Tom." (the millennial director of the stage adaptation of Vincenzo Latronico's Perfection)

Media & Culture

Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy: now with an answer key. Hunter Harris's viral quiz asked readers to tell apart the real CBS News editor-in-chief from Succession's favorite failson, and the answers are as damning as the setup. Her real quotes read like parody. So do his. The line between the trade press and prestige TV has officially dissolved. (Hunter Harris)

The studio deal is real life imitating TV. Skydance's purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery closed Tuesday, uniting two historic movie studios under David Ellison, whose biggest backer is his father, Oracle founder Larry Ellison. Ellison had only ever run one media company before (Skydance Media). Now he controls Paramount, The Free Press, CBS News, and two studios. Kendall Roy could never. (Hunter Harris)

Monday Scaries is the best Halloween programming in town. Feed Me is hosting three scary movie nights at Cobble Hill Cinemas this month, with $10 tickets that include popcorn, a drink, and a surprise intro from a "Friend of Feed Me." The lineup: The Vanishing on Oct 12, Trick 'r Treat on Oct 19, and Creep on Oct 26. Autumnal movie culture at its most civilized. (Feed Me)

Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Canadian poet took the top honor this week, which means it is now socially acceptable for all the fair-weather fans to act like they have always loved her dense, strange, gorgeous work. Time to dust off Autobiography of Red. (Feed Me)

The saddest millennial novel of last year is now a Berlin play. Vincenzo Latronico's Perfection, a short novel about two thinly sketched millennial expats in 2010s Berlin with almost no dialogue and pages of apartment descriptions, has been staged with the audience sitting under bright lights, implicated. The millennial director says all of Berlin hates the characters but all of Berlin is the characters. Ouch. (Feed Me)

Tech & Platforms

Hasan Piker is an important political force now, whether you like it or not. The Twitch streamer commands an audience that traditional campaigns would kill for, and streaming is apparently winning the midterms. Politics does not happen on cable news anymore. It happens in a chat window. (SIC)

Grindr is a $3 billion company that lobbies Washington. The hookup app has gone full institution: public markets, a massive valuation, and a policy shop. Tech interests figured out how tech media works, and now they are figuring out how Congress works. (SIC)

The millennial internet is dead and politicians killed it. A new essay argues social media use is declining and what is left has shifted from conversation to passive scrolling. Algorithms and short-form video drove the engagement, and they also made it easier to quit. Everyone is a lurker now. (SIC)

Gen Z thinks sports betting is investing. That is the claim in a new roundup of gambling-era economics, and the punchline is that their bank balances tell a very different story. Prediction markets, crypto, sportsbooks: Max Read's theory that everything became gambling is getting easier to believe every week. (SIC)

ChatGPT is putting real cartoonists' signatures on fake New Yorker cartoons. The bots are not just stealing the style now, they are forging the byline. For actual illustrators, this is the nightmare scenario in one headline. (SIC)

Money & Status

Everything became gambling, and Max Read wrote the theory. Read argues that crypto, prediction markets, sports, politics, and AI are all downstream of the same shift: probabilistic thinking colonizing every part of life. Nate Silver calls this crowd "The River." Once you internalize the theory, you start seeing the ugly throughline everywhere. (Feed Me)

Only 31% of adults think college is very important. That Gallup number keeps falling, and the credential economy keeps wobbling. One enterprising response: need help paying for college? Try bass fishing. Scholarships exist for it, apparently. (SIC)

Super Smalls went from a "honey, don't touch this" moment to a real business. Founder Maria Dueñas Jacobs, a former Elle accessories director and mom of three, turned her daughter's jewelry envy into a kids' brand built on the idea that opening a package should feel like a kid version of a Cartier box. Oprah has now picked it for her Favorite Things five years in a row. The busy-mom thesis holds. (Sticky Stuff)

Food & City Life

Ridgewood's Hellbender has one of New York's best young chefs, and now you know where she eats. In a Q and A, chef Yara Herrera names JR and Son her current obsession (order the shrimp scampi), Adda for the most memorable meal of the year, and Kisa as the comfort spot she almost does not want to tell you about. Her first Google search in a new city: "tacos near me." (InsideHook)

Philippe Chow just turned 20, and Monkey Bar has the best wedge salad in the city. That is the verdict from a week of very serious on-the-ground reporting: the 52nd Street restaurant's anniversary bash was full of lychee martinis and Peking duck, and around the corner the chopped wedge with boiled eggs, gorgonzola, and bacon cubes is, quote, "a salad I could eat every single day." (InsideHook)

Pershing Square is closing. The bistro across from Grand Central had the best booths and the best zip code in Midtown, but the geography alone could not save it. The fear now is that the space becomes a Sweetgreen. Pour one out for underage mimosas with your college ex. (Feed Me)

Blue Bottle changed its default milk from oat to whole. Nature is healing, the vibe shift continues, and the oat milk era is officially over. Drink your latte like it is 2019. (Feed Me)

Cities & Oddities

Tokyo's Hibiya station will play the Godzilla theme as its departure melody. Trains, giant lizards, perfect pairing. If your commute does not come with a kaiju soundtrack, is it even a commute? (SIC)

Paris is letting Louis Vuitton redevelop two streets at the foot of its future Champs-Elysees flagship. A city handing its most famous boulevard to a luxury brand is either peak Paris or the end of it. (SIC)

A 90-foot lava-rock arch collapsed in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. A tropical storm tore through the park and took down one of its most stunning formations, cut from a lava flow about 550 years old. A reminder to enjoy the nature around you, because it is changing constantly. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Eva Marie Saint died Tuesday at 102. The On the Waterfront star lived gloriously long; even her Times obit writer Aljean Harmetz is 96. (Feed Me)

• The New Museum Triennial is back, and it is more international than ever. (SIC)

• Knickerbocker Avenue in Brooklyn will temporarily be "Alvarado Ave" in honor of Knicks guard Jose Alvarado. (SIC)

• PlayUncle Farti and the rise of the Spotify burner account: anonymous accounts are quietly shaping how music gets discovered. (SIC)

• Google unveiled "Playground," bringing AI gaming to tens of millions of creators. An all-you-can-play buffet. (SIC)

• Rattails are allegedly back. One editor claims to have borne witness yesterday. (SIC)

• The internet runs on cats and porn, and it is about to get cattier: hundreds of new top-level domains could be added, including .meow and .fart. (SIC)

• A low resting heart rate is the new fitness flex. Bradycardia is in. (SIC)

• The LACMA Calder Erewhon smoothie is what the art world deserves. Museum swag has jumped the shark and landed in the juice bar. (SIC)

Thursday, October 8, 2026 — Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $194 million: the amount a former CIA officer admitted to stealing, including 298 gold bars worth about $46 million

• $1.3 million: what a $30 estate sale painting just sold for at auction

• 70 million: Trump Accounts auto-enrolled for kids since July; only about 8 million have been claimed

• 17%: Americans who approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living, per AP-NORC

• 41 of 62: Republican candidates in competitive races who have broken with Trump or downplayed the connection, per Reuters

• $105: oil topped this level on fresh Middle East fears

• 19.6% vs 6.7%: Google's unreleased Gemini Argon 4 vs Claude Fable on a legal skills benchmark

• 15%: Argon 4's hallucination rate, vs 45% for GPT-6 Astra and 59% for Opus 5.5

• $600: what an 18-year-old allegedly paid an undercover FBI agent for an AK-47 in a Mall of America terror plot

• 350,000: Palestinians relying on one man's Telegram channel to navigate West Bank checkpoints

• $250: what Michael and Susan Dell pledged per child to 25 million kids' Trump Accounts

• 45 days: the expected length of ICE's reported "Operation Safe California" surge

• 26 years: how much older autocrats are than their median citizen, up from 19 in 1960

• 21% and 20%: the Rams' and Bills' odds to reach the Super Bowl

Quotes of the Day

• "It's not that the Chinese have not replicated TSMC. They have not replicated ASML. That's the limiting factor." — Elon Musk, on the true chokepoint in chips

• "If you're not worried, you're living in a cave." — Sen. Jim Justice, on the GOP's midterm mood

• "In a few decades, as biotechnology continues to develop, human organs will continue to be transplanted and people will become younger and perhaps even achieve immortality." — Vladimir Putin, caught on a hot mic with Xi Jinping

• "Public shareholders are going to benefit from the rise in this stock." — Blue Owl co-CEO Marc Lipschultz, after shares fell 70%

• "All we really are determining is: are Microsoft and Amazon going to pay their bills?" — Lipschultz, brushing off AI bubble fears

• "They have life; they've seen the world." — Matthieu Blazy, on why his couture show was half models over 40

AI & The Machines

Google's Gemini Argon 4 is crushing benchmarks and you can't use it yet. DeepMind gave it to select testers last week and the numbers turned heads. It scored 19.6% on Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark vs 6.7% for Claude Fable. It beat its nearest rival by nearly 10 points on Zapier's AutomationBench, which tests everyday business tasks like CRM, bookkeeping, and onboarding. Its hallucination rate came in at 15%, far below GPT-6 Astra (45%) and Opus 5.5 (59%). On LMArena it is now neck and neck with Claude, which has dominated the rankings all year. The bigger point: Google is building AI for its millions of business users, not for coders, and it might be working. (TechCrunch, Google's blog)

ChatGPT is getting a visual makeover. OpenAI is rolling out an "Intelligent UI" for all users that generates interactive elements inside chatbot answers. More show, less tell. (WIRED)

Three engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a real Toyota Corolla. The mission: drive to In-N-Out. Only one of them made it. (WIRED)

A startup wants to make water from air using data centers' waste heat. Atoco's new machines use specialized materials to harvest water from some of the driest air on Earth, with no electricity needed. (WIRED)

The big hacks won't come from AI labs. They'll come from criminals with a few hundred thousand dollars in GPUs. Meta's former security chief Alex Stamos sketched the scenario: America's 4,000-plus community banks "do not run their own software security team." Drop-ship the GPUs through an Emirati address to Russia, where cooling is easy ("you open up the window, right?"), and go. JPMorgan might survive an AI agent swarm. Your local bank won't. (Semafor)

Money & Power

Blue Owl's co-CEOs say the market has them all wrong. After redemptions fed a backlash against private credit and the stock fell 70%, Marc Lipschultz and Doug Ostrover made a rare joint appearance on Semafor's Compound Interest podcast. They dismissed the idea of a management buyout ("we went public for a reason and that reason stands") and promised "fantastic results" over the next 18 months. (Semafor)

The global bond selloff is structural, not just about France. Borrowing costs are rising for governments everywhere, even ones with slim deficits. Mark Burgess, who chairs the investment committee of an Australian retirement giant, called it "a very structural break inside the most important market in the world." The AI twist: hyperscalers are financing decades-long buildouts to match, with Meta selling 30- and 40-year bonds and Google issuing a rare century bond. "The long end of the yield curve is a dangerous place right now." (Semafor)

ASML went from expecting flat growth to chasing a backlog out to 2028, "maybe beyond." CEO Christophe Fouquet told the Hello Tomorrow summit that six months ago the chip equipment giant saw a flat 2026 and 2027. Now AI demand has flipped the picture. Given ASML's place in the supply chain, that's about as strong a demand signal as exists. (Fireside Alpha)

The friendly activist wants Mattel to sell itself. Ariel Investments' John Rogers, a longtime consigliere to CEOs from Obama to Howard Schultz, wrote an activist-tinged letter urging Mattel to find a buyer. With another activist in the mix, holders of more than 9% of shares are pushing for a sale. Authentic Brands, owner of Reebok and Nine West, has expressed interest. (Semafor)

The Trump administration is investigating Wells Fargo for trying to increase Black homeownership. The efforts date to 2022 and came in response to Biden-era pressure on big lenders. The letter to CEO Charlie Scharf is a warning about how today's corporate positioning gets punished when the political pendulum swings. Democrats could take a chamber next month and run the same play in reverse. (Semafor)

A $30 estate sale painting just sold for $1.3 million. A Michigan treasure hunter bought a painting of shells at a local physician's estate sale. It turned out to be Gertrude Abercrombie's 1951 "Alderman Merriam's Shells," which the artist had traded to the doctor in exchange for medical services. (Numlock)

The Midterms & Washington

Nate Silver took AOC first in his 2028 Democratic primary draft. On Still Counting EP5, Silver argued the left's fortunes are rising and 2028 matters because it is the first open nomination in both parties since 2012 without Trump on the ballot. Each party gets a rare chance to redefine itself. (Silver Bulletin)

Republicans are approaching November like passengers who just saw the captain put on a parachute. AP-NORC found just 17% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living. A Reuters review of 62 competitive congressional races found 41 GOP candidates, roughly two-thirds, have broken with Trump on issues or deemphasized their ties. Trump told voters to treat the midterms like he's on the ballot. The candidates are acting like he isn't. (Counterpoint)

WIRED's midterms to watch: data centers, Musk money, and the AI lobby. The 2026 midterms are "the most WIRED elections yet." Also in the issue: an interactive where you get to spend Elon Musk's money yourself. (WIRED)

Every kid in America now has a Trump Account. Almost nobody has claimed theirs. At a White House event, Trump marked the auto-enrollment of all 70 million kids under 18 with Social Security numbers. The Dells pledged $250 each to 25 million children. But a parent still has to claim the account to get the one-time $1,000 federal deposit, and only about 8 million, roughly 10%, have been claimed. The money stays locked until 18, then can be used for a home or college. (Morning Briefing)

ICE is reportedly running a secret 45-day surge across California. "Operation Safe California" began near San Diego and is expected to push through Los Angeles to San Francisco by November. Officers were told to arrest every unauthorized immigrant they encounter, not just those with records. One source texted "management want numbers." Officers are on mandatory six-day weeks with time off canceled. DHS won't confirm or deny. (Morning Briefing)

Law & Disorder

A former CIA officer admitted to stealing nearly $194 million. David J. Rush, 49, a senior executive with top-secret clearance, fabricated classified programs to divert the money. The FBI recovered 298 gold bars (about $46 million), $2 million in cash, and more than 30 luxury watches, plus Florida mansions bought with $145 million in wire transfers. He also admitted leaking details of a US clandestine source to a foreign official. He had lied about his education and military record to join the agency in 2009. He faces up to 20 years. (Morning Briefing)

The FBI says it stopped an ISIS-inspired shooting plot at the Mall of America. Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, allegedly paid $600 to an undercover agent for an AK-47-style rifle (inoperable) and four magazines with live ammo. Prosecutors say he pledged allegiance to ISIS on video and named October 24, when a Hmong arts celebration would draw "a lot of people." The case started in late 2024 when he talked about joining al Shabaab in Somalia, then allegedly decided he couldn't afford the trip, "so i will do attack here." (Morning Briefing)

A Nigerian national found exposed near a Pennsylvania park said he was handing out flyers for a Democrat. Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe told police he was waiting to canvass for congressional candidate Janelle Stelson, who is running against Rep. Scott Perry. He pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct and ICE took him into custody October 1. He had overstayed his visa since November 2019. Her campaign says it never heard of him, though materials in his car linked him to canvassing. (Morning Briefing)

The Culture

Fashion loves a wrinkle. Laurel Pantin came back from Paris Fashion Week obsessed with imperfection: wrinkles pressed into the clothes at Celine, charmingly undone styling at Polo, and runways where a quarter of the models were 40 or older. Her read is that it's bigger than a trend. It's a backlash against AI polish, a new premium on "evidence of the hand." The polish is awful, she writes, and it's subconsciously making everyone want something tactile and a little messed up. (Earl Earl)

What if dictators never died? Jerusalem Demsas went into the longevity science and came out surprised: autopsies of 40 centenarians found every single death attributable to disease, which means curing disease could theoretically keep bodies going for centuries. Then the hot mic: Xi musing that "you are still a child at 70," Putin dreaming of endless organ transplants and immortality. Autocrats already skew 26 years older than their citizens, up from 19 in 1960, because they never leave. Imagine if they never had to. (The Argument)

Men are more loyal to their barbers than their romantic partners. The stat comes from a dumb survey, but InsideHook's editor says the core truth holds. He's had two barbers in his life; the current one has cut his hair every six weeks for eight years. In an era of faceless transactions, the barber chair might be one of the last "old world" male relationships, and men losing friends as they age are clinging to it. (InsideHook)

Your balance peaks at 30. Eyes closed, 28. A Japanese study found that's when it starts slipping, earlier than you'd think. The good news: it's trainable, and a new fitness toy might help. (InsideHook)

The University of Arizona just paused nearly all frat activity. Almost half the school's fraternities are facing unspecified misconduct allegations. The Dean of Students called the number and severity of cases "egregious." (Pirate Wires)

NYC Mayor Mamdani spent the October 7 anniversary talking about Gaza. On the third anniversary of the Hamas attacks, Mamdani condemned "the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza" and US funding of it, with a brief nod to the actual victims. Pirate Wires' response: bro just fix the schools. (Pirate Wires)

The rationalists are fighting about dueling. Scott Alexander admitted his debate challenge to Steven Pinker wasn't about truth-seeking. He wanted to battle him publicly, "as duels were no longer legal," because Pinker had insulted him by disagreeing. Pirate Wires wonders: if you truly believed the world was ending, would you spend this much energy on your ego? Maybe "the world is ending" just became an identity. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Chip City Cookies is closing all locations, including Hoboken and Montclair. (Hoboken Girl)

• Timex just redesigned the Ironman. The Retroware Digital keeps the alarm and chronograph, goes full retro-future, and sizes up to 46mm. (Cool Supply)

• The new James Bond game is actually worth finishing. "First Light" nails the gadgets, the sneaking, and the sarcastic backtalk, with stealth plus the occasional full Rambo moment. (Cool Supply)

• The Supreme Court declined the Post-it note inventor's case. Alan Amron says he came up with the sticky note in 1973 and 3M stole it. Three decades of lawsuits end here. (Semafor)

• Tristan Harris's Center for Humane Technology is laying off most staff and going "founder-led" after years of internal tension over direction. (WIRED)

• The Social Reckoning, Sorkin's Facebook sequel, "attempts to shame a ruling class that has proved itself shameless." (WIRED)

• A Tennessee woman survived two lethal injections, per Eddie Huang's podcast. Somehow that sentence needed no embellishment. (Canal Street Dreams)

• Prediction markets give Jay-Z a 47% chance of playing the Super Bowl halftime show. (Sherwood)

• Inside Warren Buffett's YouTube rabbit hole: Glenn Close clips, 1950s commercials, and Uzbekistan's version of America's Got Talent. The algorithm gets us all. (Sherwood)

• Plum Sykes ranked coffee table books. Most are brand catalogues with no point of view. The exception worth buying before it sells out: Simon Upton's "A-Z Interiors." (Plum Sykes)

• This weekend in Hoboken and Jersey City: 100+ events including RENT the musical, a women's wellness fair, autumn yoga in the park, and an artisan market with adoptable dogs. (Hoboken Girl)

midday.body:
Thursday, October 8, 2026: Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 194: the age of Jonathan, the world's oldest living land animal. Scientists just sequenced the genome of the 194-year-old tortoise and found unique gene variants in most aging pathways, including DNA repair. Sorry, longevity influencers: you probably can't copy him.

• 91: pounds of meth in Melissa Kyle's car. A federal judge ruled the Flock license plate search that led to the bust was an unconstitutional warrantless search, so all of it gets thrown out. Now 404 Media has the bodycam footage.

• 250,000: the crowd that watched Ginette Reno and Celine Dion sing "Un peu plus haut, un peu plus loin" for Quebec's 400th anniversary in 2008. Designer Ruby Thelot's pick of the day.

• 60: the battles the Duke of Wellington fought across India, Iberia, and Waterloo without losing a major one. His secret, per The Daily General: he was the better guesser.

• 6: meters underground, where Open Ground nightclub sits in a converted WWII bunker in Wuppertal, Germany. DJ Yu Su called it possibly the best club night of her 2026.

• 2,680,135: holes drilled into wood paneling at Klymax, the Bali club DJ Harvey built with Potato Head. The perforations diffuse sound across the dancefloor.

• 500: the sweet spot crowd at Klymax. Big enough for the room to lose itself together, small enough that the DJ doesn't have to play the easy hits.

• 100: decibels, the level Open Ground's main room rarely crossed. Quieter than almost any club Yu Su has played, yet full of textural detail.

• 2013: the year the Black Vault filed the FOIA request that just surfaced the CIA's internal talking points on the Bin Laden raid. A decade-plus wait for paperwork.

Quotes of the Day

• "All the business of war, and indeed all the business of life, is to endeavour to find out what you don't know by what you do; that's what I called guessing what was at the other side of the hill." (Duke of Wellington, via The Daily General)

• "Nothing in that room asks you to brace." (DJ Yu Su, on Open Ground nightclub, via Why Is This Interesting?)

• "Feed art in one end, and happy people come out the other." (DJ Harvey, on his Bali club Klymax, via Why Is This Interesting?)

• "A club sells a feeling it can never serve directly." (Colin Nagy, Why Is This Interesting?)

Surveillance & Power

404 Media got the bodycam footage from the Flock search a judge ruled unconstitutional. Last week a federal judge said the license plate reader search of Melissa Kyle was "indiscriminate mass surveillance" and tossed the evidence, including 91 pounds of meth. Now you can watch the stop yourself. The footage shows a Tulsa County deputy driving 60 mph with one hand on the wheel and the other on his laptop, running Flock before he'd even finished pulling her over. Reading about a ruling is one thing. Seeing the search is another. (404 Media)

ICE has been investigating hundreds of nonprofits that help people register to vote. Democracy Docket reports the agency dug into voter-registration groups looking for noncitizen voting, which investigators almost never actually find. The read from 404 Media: ICE is buying tools and data access under the pretense of "voter fraud," a label it then uses to justify mass actions. Investigating hundreds of groups that get people to vote is a strange use of resources. (Democracy Docket, via 404 Media)

The AI Economy

Harvard researchers found AI coding assistants boost productivity, but the gains don't reach the bottom line. The study looked at coding assistants and agents and concluded that "productivity gains do not fully pass through to changes in software output or employment." For agents specifically, more time goes to reviewing code, and there is more code to review. The machines write faster. Humans still have to read it all. (404 Media)

McDonald's is being sued for allegedly using AI to set menu prices. The federal lawsuit claims the chain built an "information-sharing pricing platform" that draws on millions of daily transactions to set prices across thousands of US restaurants, amounting to "algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin." It started because Michael Thomas, an Illinois man, noticed his usual Quarter Pounder with cheese, fries, and Coke cost different amounts at different locations near his home. McDonald's says the suit is full of inaccuracies. (Associated Press, via 404 Media)

How We Live

The Duke of Wellington never lost a major battle because he was the better guesser. That's the argument in The Daily General today. Wellington rode the ground himself, studied his opponents' habits, hid his forces on reverse slopes, and constantly revised his picture of what the other commander intended. His method had three parts: squeeze everything out of the visible evidence, model the mind across from you, and keep score of your guesses afterward. Most people fail at both ends, the piece argues. The best nightclub in the world right now might sit in a WWII bunker in Wuppertal. Meet Jonathan, the 194-year-old tortoise who might know the secret to not dying. afternoon.body:
Thursday, October 8, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• **$192 million**: the NFL's bet on flag football. More than 100,000 girls played at US high schools last year, up 48% from the year before and 550% over five years. The NCAA recognizes women's flag in January, and the sport debuts at the 2028 Olympics.

• **$1,495,000**: the asking price of a flying saucer for sale in California. Not a metaphor.

• **7**: the hours of a marathon April 2023 meeting where Lightspeed's co-leaders told partners to clear their calendars and remake the firm for the AI era, after missing OpenAI, ElevenLabs, and Hugging Face.

• **5**: the years in a row kids' jewelry brand Super Smalls has been picked for Oprah's Favorite Things, starting with its Make It Super DIY Bead Kit in 2021.

• **1,300**: the young performers hitmaker Freddy Wexler auditioned before landing on the five teens in boy band Just Your Type. They test-ran the group on 15,000-plus phone-less summer campers.

• **724,000**: the views on one tweet ("cant explain it but i think we're going to return to dressing like this") that has After School calling a serious vibe shift.

Quotes of the Day

• "Suddenly, flag is life" (Crystal Wilson, on her 12-year-old daughter Kennedy's flag football obsession)

• "If there's one person in the world I wouldn't bet against now, it's Bari Weiss" (Caitlin Flanagan, one year ago, on the eve of the Weiss era at CBS News)

• "We are in an arms race of content output, whether we like it or not" (Liam James Ward, founder of agency Something Something, on fake TikTok fan accounts)

• "It shows someone who wants this woman to pay for the rest of her life" (First Amendment lawyer Aaron Minc, on the influencer apology settlement)

• "Nowadays, it's all about your social presence" (George Davies, 15, on his unlikely rise to a Ralph Lauren runway)

• "Motherhood made me a better founder because it taught me that delegating is a superpower" (Maria Dueñas Jacobs, founder of Super Smalls)

The Culture Machine

The NFL's $192 million bet on flag football is paying off with teen girls. More than 100,000 young women played the sport at their high schools last year. That is a 48% jump from the year before and a more than 550% increase over five years. On the field, jeweled mouth guards and mirrored Oakleys are everywhere. Oakley has launched its own elite girls' tournament, hoping to win "fans for life." With the NCAA set to recognize women's flag in January and a 2028 Olympic debut ahead, the pipeline is real. (Bloomberg)

A 15-year-old kid from Tribeca talked his way onto a Ralph Lauren runway. George Davies started hitting streetwear pop-ups at 11. In eighth grade he asked a brand contact if he could hide in the ventilation to watch the show, and staff cast him instead. He stumbled onto Aimé Leon Dore's website during a boring math class, kept showing up at the store, and founder Teddy Santis put him in a campaign. A viral street-interview video then brought him "ten different emails from different agencies and managers." (The Cut)

Hitmaker Freddy Wexler is building a boy band the old way: 1,300 auditions, five teenagers, ten months of training. After relocating the teens to Los Angeles, Just Your Type toured summer camps across New York, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts. They played for more than 15,000 phone-less campers, the most captive audience on earth. Wexler thinks the old boy-band formula "only works today if it's real," which is a funny thing to say about a group carefully engineered by a record exec. (Billboard)

A lot of "stan pages" on TikTok are run by professionals on record label payrolls. After backlash over Geese hiring the agency Chaotic Good to push its music into algorithms, Dazed reports that many fancam accounts are agency work. One account with suspiciously good photo-pit access at sombr shows is widely suspected of being one of them. Liam James Ward of agency Something Something admits to "pumping out edits" on Buffy the Vampire Slayer fan accounts his agency created, and notes fans now worry they can't tell "what's real or not anymore." (Dazed)

An influencer lost a six-year defamation suit and now owes a scripted apology plus $500 a month for 40 years. Emily Gellis, a lifestyle creator, must keep a six-minute apology video (one commenter likened it to a hostage video) pinned to the top of her Instagram and Facebook for three and a half years. She will pay Tanya Zuckerbrot, the dietitian behind the pre-Ozempic F-Factor diet, $500 a month until she is 95. (The New York Times)

Media Moves

One year into the Bari Weiss era at CBS, the ratings are in the toilet. On the eve of the Weiss era, Caitlin Flanagan wrote that she wouldn't bet against her. She meant it personally: she later left the Atlantic to work for Weiss at the Free Press. Now CBS Mornings, the Evening News, and 60 Minutes all sit in what Rusty Foster calls "the toilet." Also this week, Paramount's purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery closed on Tuesday. Hunter Harris has a full recap of Weiss's adventures on West 57th Street, ending with a quiz: "Who said that: Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy?" (Today in Tabs)

Jessica Bennett's investigation into the Amy Griffin memoir controversy is the read of the week. Delia Cai says the structure of Bennett's feature on the controversy behind venture capitalist Amy Griffin's bestselling 2025 memoir The Tell, about recovered memories of child abuse, is "incredibly damning," and urges readers to stop and read it before anything else. (Deez Links)

The Atlantic keeps hiring every remaining journalist. In its ongoing quest to employ everyone in the business, the Atlantic just hired Kevin Roose and Mike Isaac. It also let Alexandra Petri write a poem instead of jokes, and she turns out to be good at that too. On the other hand, it published a schmaltzy profile of an Ohio trucker described as "a lifelong Democrat who had voted for Trump for the first time in 2024." Rusty Foster suggests someone should have googled him first. (Today in Tabs)

The AI Economy

Lightspeed missed AI's early days, so it remade itself in a single seven-hour meeting. In April 2023, months after ChatGPT launched, co-leaders Ravi Mhatre and Bejul Somaia told partners to clear their calendars, even board meetings. The firm had missed OpenAI (rival Khosla had an early stake), ElevenLabs, and Hugging Face. The question on the table: if AI is going to change everything, what would it mean to act as though that were true? Partners broke into subgroups, and the Europeans and Israelis stayed on past midnight. Now the firm is remade and poised to score with Anthropic, with PE-style roll-ups in the mix. (Newcomer)

The people who drink their own pee are obsessed with AI. Futurism's Joe Wilkins reports that urine drinkers use AI to reassure themselves it is a miraculous cure-all. Rusty Foster notes this is nearly identical to an exaggerated satire he wrote last December about the AI industry ("They took the lathe of heaven away from me, and they were right to"). Also in AI this week: chatbots have worse security flaws than we knew, and John Herrman wonders if the worst outcome of "exceptionally capable personal agents" is them working as promised. (Today in Tabs)

How We Live

Super Smalls founder Maria Dueñas Jacobs turned "honey, don't touch that" into a toy brand. The former Elle accessories and jewelry director started the kids' jewelry brand out of her New York apartment after her daughter Luna kept grabbing her jewelry. She wanted opening a Super Smalls box to feel like a kid's Cartier unboxing. Oprah's Favorite Things has picked the brand five years running, and selling in the Amazon store became a real growth channel. Her founder lesson: kids see the hard stretches too, not just the wins, and that shapes them. (The Sticky Stuff)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Prime Day is officially over, but most of the big deals are still live on Amazon, from Apple to Breville to iRobot (InsideHook)

• Rex Jr., possibly "the most important T. rex that has or will ever be found," was discovered in Wyoming (Today in Tabs)

• A 50-foot bronze rendition of the Titan Prometheus sits just outside the legal borders of Starbase, Texas (Today in Tabs)

• The secret home of Tabasco sauce is on Avery Island (yes, that one) (Today in Tabs)

• A potato, arriving in your backyard by drone (Today in Tabs)

• Goth Ranch by Clorox, exclusively at Walmart (Today in Tabs)

• Fandeliers? Chandefans? "Chaos, it seems, reigns in fanville" (Today in Tabs)

• Test your word-nerd knowledge in Etymystery, and get ready for November with Voting Simulator 3D from The Onion (Today in Tabs)

• Pop bits: Olivia Rodrigo covers The Hollywood Reporter, Harry Styles interviews Thom Yorke for Rolling Stone, Tate McRae's next single is called "Housewife," and a Bridgerton spin-off about a young Lady Violet is in the works at Netflix (After School)

evening.body:
Thursday, October 8, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• **90-foot**: the height of the lava-rock arch that collapsed this week in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park after a tropical storm tore through. The Park Service says it was cut from a 550-year-old lava flow. Nature does not sit still.

• **31%**: the share of U.S. adults who now say a college education is "very important," per a new Gallup survey. A credential that used to be a given is now a genuine debate.

• **42 minutes**: how long it took Glastonbury to sell out this year. Ticket inflation is real and the frenzy is back.

• **$100M**: the value of art Jeff Koons is reportedly selling from his personal collection. When the market gets shaky, the trophy room gets sold.

• **30%**: the jump in print and digital subscriptions at Georgia's Monticello News, six weeks after 25-year-old Evan Newton bought the paper with his entire savings. Local news might be boring, but it is necessary (his words).

• **230mg**: the caffeine packed into a 10-gummy pack of Five-Hour Energy's new candy-style gummies. Halloween candy for your friend who crushes Celsius all day.

• **$3 billion**: Grindr is now a $3 billion company, and it is lobbying Washington. The hookup app has a K Street playbook.

Quotes of the Day

• "Let's do the fucking news!" (Bari Weiss, the real answer in Hunter Harris's "Who Said That: Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy" quiz)

• "If you want something done, give it to a busy mom." (Maria Dueñas Jacobs, founder of Super Smalls, in a founder interview)

• "exclusivity is not the objective" (Arnaud Frisch, founder of Paris nightclub Silencio, on what makes a nightclub an institution)

• "everyone everywhere is just trying to make One Big Bet and Get Rich Quick" (Emily Sundberg, summarizing Max Read's theory that everything is gambling now)

• "All of Berlin hates Anna and Tom, but all of Berlin also is Anna and Tom." (the millennial director of the stage adaptation of Vincenzo Latronico's Perfection)

Media & Culture

Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy: now with an answer key. Hunter Harris's viral quiz asked readers to tell apart the real CBS News editor-in-chief from Succession's favorite failson, and the answers are as damning as the setup. Her real quotes read like parody. So do his. The line between the trade press and prestige TV has officially dissolved. (Hunter Harris)

The studio deal is real life imitating TV. Skydance's purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery closed Tuesday, uniting two historic movie studios under David Ellison, whose biggest backer is his father, Oracle founder Larry Ellison. Ellison had only ever run one media company before (Skydance Media). Now he controls Paramount, The Free Press, CBS News, and two studios. Kendall Roy could never. (Hunter Harris)

Monday Scaries is the best Halloween programming in town. The lineup: The Vanishing on Oct 12, Trick 'r Treat on Oct 19, and Creep on Oct 26. Autumnal movie culture at its most civilized. (Feed Me)

Vincenzo Latronico's Perfection, a short novel about two thinly sketched millennial expats in 2010s Berlin with almost no dialogue and pages of apartment descriptions, has been staged with the audience sitting under bright lights, implicated. Hasan Piker is an important political force now, whether you like it or not. The Twitch streamer commands an audience that traditional campaigns would kill for, and streaming is apparently winning the midterms. Politics does not happen on cable news anymore. It happens in a chat window. (SIC)

Grindr is a $3 billion company that lobbies Washington. The hookup app has gone full institution: public markets, a massive valuation, and a policy shop. Tech interests figured out how tech media works, and now they are figuring out how Congress works. (SIC)

Algorithms and short-form video drove the engagement, and they also made it easier to quit. Everyone is a lurker now. (SIC)

Prediction markets, crypto, sportsbooks: Max Read's theory that everything became gambling is getting easier to believe every week. (SIC)

ChatGPT is putting real cartoonists' signatures on fake New Yorker cartoons. The bots are not just stealing the style now, they are forging the byline. For actual illustrators, this is the nightmare scenario in one headline. (SIC)

Super Smalls went from a "honey, don't touch this" moment to a real business. Oprah has now picked it for her Favorite Things five years in a row. The busy-mom thesis holds. (Sticky Stuff)

Food & City Life

Ridgewood's Hellbender has one of New York's best young chefs, and now you know where she eats. In a Q and A, chef Yara Herrera names JR and Son her current obsession (order the shrimp scampi), Adda for the most memorable meal of the year, and Kisa as the comfort spot she almost does not want to tell you about. Her first Google search in a new city: "tacos near me." (InsideHook)

Philippe Chow just turned 20, and Monkey Bar has the best wedge salad in the city. That is the verdict from a week of very serious on-the-ground reporting: the 52nd Street restaurant's anniversary bash was full of lychee martinis and Peking duck, and around the corner the chopped wedge with boiled eggs, gorgonzola, and bacon cubes is, quote, "a salad I could eat every single day." (InsideHook)

Pershing Square is closing. The bistro across from Grand Central had the best booths and the best zip code in Midtown, but the geography alone could not save it. The fear now is that the space becomes a Sweetgreen. Pour one out for underage mimosas with your college ex. (Feed Me)

Blue Bottle changed its default milk from oat to whole. Nature is healing, the vibe shift continues, and the oat milk era is officially over. Drink your latte like it is 2019. (Feed Me)

Cities & Oddities

Tokyo's Hibiya station will play the Godzilla theme as its departure melody. Trains, giant lizards, perfect pairing. If your commute does not come with a kaiju soundtrack, is it even a commute? (SIC)

Paris is letting Louis Vuitton redevelop two streets at the foot of its future Champs-Elysees flagship. A city handing its most famous boulevard to a luxury brand is either peak Paris or the end of it. (SIC)

A 90-foot lava-rock arch collapsed in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. A tropical storm tore through the park and took down one of its most stunning formations, cut from a lava flow about 550 years old. A reminder to enjoy the nature around you, because it is changing constantly. (InsideHook)

• Eva Marie Saint died Tuesday at 102. The On the Waterfront star lived gloriously long; even her Times obit writer Aljean Harmetz is 96. (Feed Me)

• The New Museum Triennial is back, and it is more international than ever. (SIC)

• Knickerbocker Avenue in Brooklyn will temporarily be "Alvarado Ave" in honor of Knicks guard Jose Alvarado. (SIC)

• PlayUncle Farti and the rise of the Spotify burner account: anonymous accounts are quietly shaping how music gets discovered. (SIC)

• Google unveiled "Playground," bringing AI gaming to tens of millions of creators. An all-you-can-play buffet. (SIC)

• Rattails are allegedly back. One editor claims to have borne witness yesterday. (SIC)

• The internet runs on cats and porn, and it is about to get cattier: hundreds of new top-level domains could be added, including .meow and .fart. (SIC)

• A low resting heart rate is the new fitness flex. Bradycardia is in. (SIC)

• The LACMA Calder Erewhon smoothie is what the art world deserves. Museum swag has jumped the shark and landed in the juice bar. (SIC)

The millennial internet is dead and politicians killed it.

A new essay argues social media use is declining and what is left has shifted from conversation to passive scrolling. Algorithms and short-form video drove the engagement, and they also made it easier to quit. Everyone is a lurker now. (
SIC
Gen Z thinks sports betting is investing.

That is the claim in a new roundup of gambling-era economics, and the punchline is that their bank balances tell a very different story. Prediction markets, crypto, sportsbooks: Max Read's theory that everything became gambling is getting easier to believe every week. (
SIC
ChatGPT is putting real cartoonists' signatures on fake New Yorker cartoons.
The bots are not just stealing the style now, they are forging the byline. For actual illustrators, this is the nightmare scenario in one headline. (
SIC
Money & Status
Everything became gambling, and Max Read wrote the theory.

Read argues that crypto, prediction markets, sports, politics, and AI are all downstream of the same shift: probabilistic thinking colonizing every part of life. Nate Silver calls this crowd "The River." Once you internalize the theory, you start seeing the ugly throughline everywhere. (
Feed Me
Only 31% of adults think college is very important.
That Gallup number keeps falling, and the credential economy keeps wobbling. One enterprising response: need help paying for college? Try bass fishing. Scholarships exist for it, apparently. (
SIC
Super Smalls went from a "honey, don't touch this" moment to a real business.

Founder Maria Dueñas Jacobs, a former Elle accessories director and mom of three, turned her daughter's jewelry envy into a kids' brand built on the idea that opening a package should feel like a kid version of a Cartier box. Oprah has now picked it for her Favorite Things five years in a row. The busy-mom thesis holds. (
Sticky Stuff
Food & City Life
Ridgewood's Hellbender has one of New York's best young chefs, and now you know where she eats.

In a Q and A, chef Yara Herrera names JR and Son her current obsession (order the shrimp scampi), Adda for the most memorable meal of the year, and Kisa as the comfort spot she almost does not want to tell you about. Her first Google search in a new city: "tacos near me." (
InsideHook
Philippe Chow just turned 20, and Monkey Bar has the best wedge salad in the city.

That is the verdict from a week of very serious on-the-ground reporting: the 52nd Street restaurant's anniversary bash was full of lychee martinis and Peking duck, and around the corner the chopped wedge with boiled eggs, gorgonzola, and bacon cubes is, quote, "a salad I could eat every single day." (
InsideHook
Pershing Square is closing.

The bistro across from Grand Central had the best booths and the best zip code in Midtown, but the geography alone could not save it. The fear now is that the space becomes a Sweetgreen. Pour one out for underage mimosas with your college ex. (
Feed Me
Blue Bottle changed its default milk from oat to whole.
Nature is healing, the vibe shift continues, and the oat milk era is officially over. Drink your latte like it is 2019. (
Feed Me
Cities & Oddities
Tokyo's Hibiya station will play the Godzilla theme as its departure melody.
Trains, giant lizards, perfect pairing. If your commute does not come with a kaiju soundtrack, is it even a commute? (
SIC
Paris is letting Louis Vuitton redevelop two streets at the foot of its future Champs-Elysees flagship.
A city handing its most famous boulevard to a luxury brand is either peak Paris or the end of it. (
SIC
A 90-foot lava-rock arch collapsed in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park.

A tropical storm tore through the park and took down one of its most stunning formations, cut from a lava flow about 550 years old. A reminder to enjoy the nature around you, because it is changing constantly. (
InsideHook
Quick Hits & Curiosities
Eva Marie Saint died Tuesday at 102. The On the Waterfront star lived gloriously long; even her Times obit writer Aljean Harmetz is 96. (
Feed Me
The New Museum Triennial is back, and it is more international than ever. (
SIC
Knickerbocker Avenue in Brooklyn will temporarily be "Alvarado Ave" in honor of Knicks guard Jose Alvarado. (
SIC
PlayUncle Farti and the rise of the Spotify burner account: anonymous accounts are quietly shaping how music gets discovered. (
SIC
Google unveiled "Playground," bringing AI gaming to tens of millions of creators. An all-you-can-play buffet. (
SIC
Rattails are allegedly back. One editor claims to have borne witness yesterday. (
SIC
The internet runs on cats and porn, and it is about to get cattier: hundreds of new top-level domains could be added, including .meow and .fart. (
SIC
A low resting heart rate is the new fitness flex. Bradycardia is in. (
SIC
The LACMA Calder Erewhon smoothie is what the art world deserves. Museum swag has jumped the shark and landed in the juice bar. (
SIC

Friday, October 9, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• $80 billion: the tower of debt Skydance took on to close its $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. Wall Street flinched. $SKYD fell nearly 3% in its first trading session, then slid another 8% in the second.

• 4.51%: how much women's elite road times improved after carbon-plated supershoes arrived, compared with 2.62% for men. By the end of 2025, not a single pre-supershoe women's 10K mark remained in the all-time top 50 (8.9% of the men's old-era marks still do).

• 55%: athletes who report at least one superstition, per a review of 27 studies. More than 90% have a sport-specific ritual, from lucky socks to a fixed warmup.

• 33: Daniel Dele-Tunji's age. The menswear veteran who has held posts at P. Johnson, Brunello Cucinelli, and Stoffa now runs his own holistic style consultancy, Studio Raisonne.

• 2024: the year chef Yara Herrera opened Hellbender in Ridgewood, Queens. It has since picked up a two-star New York Times review and an Esquire Best New Restaurants nod.

Quotes of the Day

• "Give us time, and we'll prove it." (David Ellison, addressing skeptics of the Skydance deal at his internal town hall)

• "Free Speech Is BS" (Emmanuel Macron, headlining this week's Pirate Wires pod as France and America spar over speech laws)

The Skydance Squeeze

David Ellison took his victory lap this week. After finally closing the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, a Skydance billboard went up outside Paramount's Times Square headquarters, $SKYD debuted on the New York Stock Exchange, and Ellison took questions at an internal town hall and from reporters, including Status. To detractors he said: "Give us time, and we'll prove it." But one of the deal's biggest early skeptics has been Wall Street, and cutting roughly $80 billion in debt to sustainable levels will not be easy, experts told Status. (Status)

The Power Lines crew is all over the deal's media fallout. This week's episode breaks down what Ellison told reporters about his relationship with Donald Trump, plus what could be read from his answers to Anderson Cooper at the town hall. Tech journalist Casey Newton joins to explain why he is returning to Elon Musk's X years after quitting it, and responds to a surprise message from Kara Swisher. Watch it on YouTube or listen wherever you get podcasts. (Status)

Running Lab

Supershoes helped women more than men, a new study says. Researchers compared elite road performances before and after carbon-plated supershoes arrived, using throwing events as a control for better training and nutrition. Across the 10K, half marathon, and marathon, women's performances improved 4.51% versus 2.62% for men. Another striking stat: by the end of 2025, not a single pre-supershoe women's 10K mark remained in the all-time top 50, while 8.9% of the men's old-era marks still stand. The figures describe elite trends, so individual results still vary with speed, biomechanics, comfort, and shoe design. (Six Minute Mile)

Your race-day superstitions might actually work. A review of 27 studies found about 55% of athletes report at least one superstition, and more than 90% have a sport-specific ritual. The habits may ease anxiety by creating a sense of control, and separate research suggests pre-performance routines can improve results under pressure. Sport psychologist Cindra Kamphoff offers more tools: the "learn, burn, return" method for mistakes, an "I can" or "I am" phrase for self-doubt, gold, silver, and bronze goals for several definitions of success, and fact-checking negative thoughts. (Six Minute Mile)

Style, Food & NYC

Daniel Dele-Tunji is the stylist entrepreneurs call. The 33-year-old menswear veteran has held posts at P. Johnson, Brunello Cucinelli, Stoffa, and Ven. After building out Studio Raisonne's temporary space, he broke off to start his own holistic style consultancy, helping men find their fit, sell old garments, and tailor wardrobes to changing lifestyles. Last month he hosted a West Village pop-up selling archival and vintage finds. Cool as they come, and a hell of a sharp dresser. (InsideHook)

Chef Yara Herrera names her favorite NYC bites. Her best dish of the year: head-on wild Gulf prawns drowning in habanero pineapple butter at Hellbender, her own Ridgewood spot that earned a two-star Times review and an Esquire Best New Restaurants nod since opening in 2024. Herrera, who cut her teeth at Spago and Providence, also dishes on her most memorable meal of the year, where she always lands after midnight, and her first Google search when she touches down somewhere new. (InsideHook)

Is Brandon Flowers the male Lana Del Rey? The Killers frontman performed "An American Dream" from his new album Thrasher on Jimmy Fallon, and InsideHook says the bombastic, sincere rendition recalls the great late-night moments of the past two decades. The piece asks whether Flowers has become the kind of larger-than-life pop auteur the culture used to reserve for Del Rey. (InsideHook)

InsideHook threw a party to launch its new men's style newsletter. The publication gathered a who's who of menswear heads at People's to launch Protagonist, with guest of honor Chris Fenimore. Editor-in-chief James Jung admits he never got his pic with Throwing Fits' Lawrence Schlossman, and nursed the hangover at Test, a hyped Williamsburg craft brewery. (InsideHook)

The Pirate Wires Pod

Macron took the stage to call American free speech "BS." The pod dives into the free-speech war between the US and France while France deals with riots at home. Pirate Wires also reported on the State Department's fight against censorship abroad, and @metaversehell joins to discuss how Europe's speech model is seeping into America's view of speech. (Pirate Wires)

An AI doomer battle: Steven Pinker vs. Scott Alexander. The pod stages the debate between two of the sharpest minds on either side of the AI apocalypse question. (Pirate Wires)

California in disarray, aliens on the docket. @nicolewizman1 joins to discuss the state of California's mess, and the episode closes by debating Fermi's Paradox, or what the hosts are calling Solana's Paradox. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Former 60 Minutes boss Bill Owens talks his departure (Status)

• Brendan Carr dodges a pointed question about public execution (Status)

• Netflix readies for layoffs (Status)

• Alex Gibney's 'Musk' hits theaters (Status)

• Trump's new press secretary comes with a conspiratorial streak (Status)

• ABC republishes a story while admitting errors (Status)

• The New Yorker goes live Oct 12 at 5:30 PM EDT: "What the 2026 Midterms Could Mean for American Democracy" (The New Yorker)

• James Jung's song on repeat this week: the new Axel Boman x Superpitcher cut (InsideHook)
